senses: A type of dog-race where dogs jump over hurdles to get to and return from a tennis-ball dispensing box.
Extremely low.

ety: Borrowed from French ampoule. Etymologically equivalent to amphora + -ule/-le. Doublet of ampulla.

senses: A low plain.
ety: From translingual planitia, from Latin plānitia.

senses: A traditional chocolate-based atole found in Mexico, containing panela, vanilla, anise and cinnamon.
A Cuban water-based drink, containing several spices, mixed with rum or brandy.
The act of preparing something for winter weather.
The process in which solid fats are removed from liquid edible oils by cooling, which allows such oils to be stored in a refrigerator.
A monstrous creature resembling a bear with a beak.
ety: From owl + bear. Coined by Gary Gygax in the 1970s for Dungeons & Dragons.

senses: Lasting for a short period of time.
ety: From New Latin ephemerus, from Ancient Greek ἐφήμερος (ephḗmeros), the more common form of ἐφημέριος (ephēmérios, “of, for, or during the day, living or lasting but for a day, short-lived, temporary”), from ἐπί (epí, “on”) + ἡμέρα (hēméra, “day”).

senses: To convert energy from one form to another.
To transfer or convert information from one form or medium to another.
ety: 1949, back-formation from transducer, from Latin trānsdūcō, from Latin trans (“across”, preposition) + dūcō (“lead, guide”).
examples: Much as computers must transduce input information, the nervous system must transduce sensory information before it can be analyzed internally.

senses: The application of fertilizers or other water-soluble products through an irrigation system.
ety: Blend of fertilize + irrigation or similar.

senses: A large metropolitan area containing several cities and their suburbs.
ety: Blend of metropolitan + complex, originally coined as a marketing term for the Dallas–Fort Worth conurbation.

senses: An appellation owned by a single winery.
ety: From the Middle French monopole or its etymon the Late Latin monopōlium (“a monopoly”).

senses: Engaged in piracy or plunder
examples: In one respect, as I hinted above, it is only too good, so sure of success, I mean, that you are no longer secure of any respect to your property in our freebooting America.

senses: Resembling a cyst or bladder.
A fight between cats.
ety: From cat + fight. So named because, like cats, scratching is a common defensive tactic among women, as opposed to a fistfight between men.
examples: The caterwauling from the catfight in the back yard was awful; I couldn't get to sleep until it was over.

senses: A stripe or stria.
The flute of a column.
The state or quality of being bicultural.

automatic payment
examples: Under the autopay rent collection system, most of the transactions are effected on the first working day of the month.

senses: Not yet weaned; still being suckled.
Naive, wet behind the ears, green, inexperienced.
A Haitian unit of land, 100 square pas: roughly 1.3 hectares or 3.2 acres.
ety: Borrowed from French carreau. Doublet of quarrel.
examples: In 1809 and 1814, land reform in southern and western Haiti resulted in the estimated redistribution of some 76,000 carreaux of land among 2,322 civil and military officers.

senses: An old woman.
ety: From Scots, from Scottish Gaelic cailleach.

an inferred object of someone else's consciousness
ety: From Latin ēiectum (“(that which is) thrown out”), from ēiciō (“to throw out”) (see Etymology 1). Coined by W. K. Clifford by analogy with subject and object.

senses: One who calls upon (a person, especially a god) for help, assistance or guidance.
One who appeals for validation to a (notably cited) authority.

Someone who induces as an inevitable consequence.

A small dish in which hors d'oeuvres are served.
Habit; custom; usage.
ety: From Middle English habitude, from Middle French habitude, from Latin habitūdō (“condition, plight, habit, appearance”), from habeō (“to have, hold, keep”).

senses: In Mexican languages, especially Nahuatl, a glottal stop or fricative sound.
In mostly Hispanophone countries, especially Mexico, an apostrophe-like letter (lowercase ꞌ and in some orthographies capital Ꞌ) used to represent a glottal stop.
lustre; brilliancy of a surface; used especially in ceramics to denote the peculiar metallic brilliancy seen in lustred pottery such as majolica
A voracious eater; a glutton.
ety: From Middle English ganet, gante, from Old English ganot, from Proto-West Germanic *ganat, *ganatō, from Proto-Germanic *ganatuz, *ganutô (“gander”), ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *ganzô. Cognates Cognate with Dutch gent, Middle Low German gante, German Ganter, Ganser, all “gander, male goose”.
